questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a standard cost?
options: A predetermined cost per unit of output based on expected prices and usage
The actual cost per unit incurred last period
The lowest cost per unit the business has ever achieved
The cost per unit charged to the customer
questions.why: A standard cost is set in advance as a benchmark against which actual performance is compared.
whyNot: That is the actual cost, which is compared with the standard.
That would be an ideal standard at best, and is not the definition.
That is the selling price.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines an adverse variance?
options: A variance that reduces profit because actual cost exceeds standard
Any variance greater than 10% of the standard
A variance caused by a change in the standard
questions.why: Adverse means the actual result was worse than the standard, so profit is reduced.
whyNot: That is a favourable variance.
Size determines materiality, not whether a variance is adverse.
The cause does not determine the label.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines the material usage variance?
options: The difference between standard and actual quantity used, valued at the standard price
The difference between standard and actual price, valued at the actual quantity
The total difference between standard and actual material cost
The difference between material purchased and material used
questions.why: A quantity-type variance is always valued at the standard price.
whyNot: That is the material price variance.
That is the total material variance.
That is an inventory movement, not a variance.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines the labour rate variance?
options: The difference between standard and actual wage rate, valued at the actual hours worked
The difference between standard and actual hours, valued at the standard rate
The difference between total budgeted and actual wages
The cost of overtime worked during the period
questions.why: A price-type variance is always valued at the actual quantity, here the actual hours.
whyNot: That is the labour efficiency variance.
That is the total labour variance.
Overtime premium is one possible cause of an adverse rate variance.

questions.stem: Standard price is $4.00 per kg, actual price is $3.80 and 16,200 kg were bought. What is the material price variance?
questions.why: (4.00 - 3.80) x 16,200 = $3,240 favourable, because the actual price was below standard.
whyNot: Paying less than standard is favourable, not adverse.
That values the variance at the standard quantity of 15,000 kg.
That is the standard cost of the standard quantity, not a variance.

questions.stem: Standard usage is 3 kg per unit, 5,000 units were made, 16,200 kg were used and the standard price is $4.00. What is the usage variance?
whyNot: Using more than standard is adverse.
That values the variance at the actual price of $3.80.
That is the excess in kg, not its value.

questions.stem: Using the two variances above, what is the total material variance?
questions.why: 3,240 F - 4,800 A = $1,560 adverse. Check: standard cost 15,000 x 4.00 = $60,000 against actual $61,560.
whyNot: That adds the two as if both were adverse.
The adverse usage variance is the larger of the two.
That adds the two as if both were favourable.

questions.stem: Standard rate is $9.00 per hour, actual rate is $9.30 and 9,600 hours were worked. What is the labour rate variance?
whyNot: Paying above the standard rate is adverse.
That values the variance at the standard hours of 10,000.
That is the total actual wage cost.

questions.stem: Standard is 2 hours per unit, 5,000 units were made, 9,600 hours were worked and the standard rate is $9.00. What is the efficiency variance?
whyNot: Using fewer hours than standard is favourable.
That values the variance at the actual rate of $9.30.
That is the hours saved, not their value.

questions.stem: Budgeted fixed overhead is $180,000 for 4,500 units. Actual output is 5,000 units and actual overhead is $191,000. What is the total fixed overhead variance?
whyNot: That compares actual with budget and ignores the higher output absorbed.
More was absorbed than incurred, so the variance is favourable.
That is the effect of the extra output alone, ignoring the overspend.

questions.stem: Standard variable overhead is $6 per unit, actual output is 5,000 units and actual variable overhead is $32,500. What is the variance?
whyNot: Spending more than standard is adverse.
That is the standard cost, not the variance.
That uses an incorrect calculation.

questions.stem: A favourable material price variance accompanies an adverse usage variance. What is the most likely single cause?
options: A cheaper, lower-quality material was bought and produced more wastage
The workforce was paid above the standard rate
The standard price was set too low
questions.why: This is the classic interrelated pair, and the evaluation compares the price saving with the usage loss to say whether the decision paid.
whyNot: Wage rates affect the labour variances, not material usage.
Output level does not by itself cause a usage variance per unit.
A standard set too low would make the price variance adverse.

questions.stem: Poor-quality material is bought. Which third variance is it also likely to cause?
options: An adverse labour efficiency variance, because of rework and rejects
questions.why: One purchasing decision can produce three variances, and noticing that is where the higher marks are.
whyNot: Material quality does not change the wage rate paid.
If anything, slower production reduces output and makes the overhead variance adverse.
Material quality affects how long the work takes.

questions.stem: An adverse labour rate variance accompanies a favourable efficiency variance. What is the likely cause?
options: More skilled or experienced workers were used, costing more per hour but working faster
The standard hours were set too low
questions.why: Comparing the extra wage cost with the efficiency saving shows whether the decision earned or lost money.
whyNot: Material price affects the material variances.
Overhead spending does not affect the labour rate.
A standard set too low would make the efficiency variance adverse.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines management by exception?
options: Investigating only variances significant enough to justify the management time
Investigating only adverse variances and ignoring favourable ones
Revising the standards whenever a variance arises
questions.why: A materiality threshold focuses scarce management time, and a well-run system investigates significant variances in both directions.
whyNot: Favourable variances can signal a wrong standard or a quality shortcut, so they should be investigated too.
That is the absence of control.
Standards should be revised only when conditions have genuinely changed.

questions.stem: Why is a favourable variance not automatically good news?
options: It may have been bought at the cost of a larger adverse variance elsewhere, or by sacrificing quality
Favourable variances always indicate an arithmetic error
questions.why: This is the single most valuable sentence available in this topic, because it recognises that variances interrelate.
whyNot: They usually reflect a real difference, which then needs explaining.
By definition a favourable variance increases profit.
They can and should be investigated.

questions.stem: Which type of standard is normally used in practice, and why?
options: Attainable, because it assumes efficient working with normal allowances and is therefore credible
Ideal, because it gives staff the highest possible target
Basic, because leaving it unchanged allows long-term trend comparison
Actual, because it reflects what really happened
questions.why: An attainable standard is both a fair benchmark and a target staff can believe in, which protects its motivational value.
whyNot: An ideal standard assumes perfection, is almost always missed and can demotivate.
A basic standard becomes useless for control as conditions change.
An actual cost is not a standard at all.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a possible cause of an adverse material price variance?
options: An urgent small order placed at short notice
A bulk discount obtained from a supplier
Fewer labour hours worked than standard
questions.why: Urgency removes the ability to negotiate and usually means paying more per unit.
whyNot: A bulk discount would make the price variance favourable.
Wastage affects the usage variance, not price.
Hours worked affects the labour variances.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a possible cause of an adverse labour efficiency variance?
options: A pay award above the standard rate
questions.why: Idle time means hours are paid for without output, so more hours are used than standard.
whyNot: That causes an adverse rate variance.
That affects the material price variance.
Higher output affects the fixed overhead variance.

questions.stem: Why can a favourable total fixed overhead variance be misleading?
options: It may reflect higher output absorbing more overhead rather than better cost control
Fixed overheads cannot vary at all
It always means the budget was wrong
Fixed overhead variances are never calculated
questions.why: Producing above budget absorbs extra overhead, which can more than cover an overspend, so the favourable total hides the overspending.
whyNot: Actual fixed overhead spending certainly can differ from budget.
A wrong budget is one possibility among several.
The total variance is examinable at this level.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a stage in establishing a standard costing system?
options: Setting standard quantities and prices from technical study and supplier quotations
Calculating the variances for the period
questions.why: Establishing the system means studying the process, setting standards and building the standard cost card before any variances exist.
whyNot: That comes after the system is operating.
Reporting follows calculation.
Investigation is part of using the system, not establishing it.

questions.stem: A variance recurs at a similar level every month. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The standard itself is wrong and should be reviewed
The variance should be ignored under management by exception
questions.why: Investigating a variance means checking the standard as well as the performance, and a persistent variance points at the benchmark.
whyNot: A consistent pattern points to the standard rather than to behaviour.
Repeatedly identical arithmetic errors are unlikely.
A small variance that recurs every month may matter more than one large one-off.
